primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10613687/ | Methods sections 2.2–2.3, Tables 1–3
assessment: Healthy Chinese volunteers performed odor-familiarity and smell-identification testing. The three replacement odorants were distinct synthetic chemicals, and the experimental contrast changes the test, without administering fresh thyme to people with Parkinson disease.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11502474/ | Treatment discussion and the paragraph on odorants and inflammation
assessment: The review separately discusses post-COVID olfactory treatment and lists Shirazi thyme and thymol among substances with anti-inflammatory properties. The cited Shirazi thyme use addresses asthma and does not establish fresh thyme ingestion or Parkinson olfactory severity.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12203381/ | Historic medical use and neurodegenerative disease olfaction sections
assessment: The historical account describes smelling thyme and other odors to counter seasickness or unpleasant ship odors. Separate sections discuss smell testing in neurological disease. It supplies no clinical contrast of fresh thyme ingestion on Parkinson olfactory impairment.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7019837/ | Lipid findings and Parkinson disease section, Table 11
assessment: The review discusses rice-bran tocotrienol-rich fractions for lipid endpoints and separately cites delta-tocotrienol motor activity in a Parkinson mouse model. The latter is a constituent experiment, and the human evidence concerns vitamin E rather than refined rice bran oil and measured walking.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8354181/ | Introduction, Materials and Methods, Figures 2–3
assessment: The tested treatment was hemp seed ethanol extract in chlorpromazine-exposed fruit flies. A separate citation concerns isolated rice-bran gamma-oryzanol and a fly stress model. The article's locomotor results are for hemp extract.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8155682/ | Lipid discussion and Table 6, terpenes section
assessment: The review lists flaxseed and corn oils under memory performance in toddlers. Sleep-related passages instead describe compounds such as borneol and limonene and different contexts. Neither is a Parkinson insomnia comparison with cold-pressed flaxseed oil.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11275480/ | Risk-factor and fatty-acid sections
assessment: The narrative discusses insomnia as a risk factor for neurodegeneration and separately lists flaxseed oil as a source of fatty acids. That mention supplies no treatment comparison on Parkinson insomnia.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12256702/ | Dietary Supplements P1203 and Sleep Health P2578, P2582, P2584
assessment: The flaxseed supplementation synthesis reports lipid concentrations. Separate Sleep Health passages report insomnia definitions and prevalence from surveillance and cohort studies. None compares cold-pressed flaxseed oil for Parkinson insomnia.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13099475/ | Supplement exposure definition, Table 1 and cognitive results
assessment: This longitudinal observational analysis pools fish, flaxseed and krill oils under omega-3 supplement use. Insomnia is a baseline characteristic rather than a treatment outcome. Follow-up outcomes concern cognitive decline and imaging.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13347597/ | Methods, known-groups validity and results
assessment: The study developed and validated a Parkinson patient-reported health index. Gait freezing is used as a known-groups characteristic and the comparison is part of instrument validation, without dietary caraway exposure.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9947355/ | Study table, discussion of the Phillips Parkinson trial and MCT comparison
assessment: Canola oil was the comparator in a separate MCT crossover in Alzheimer disease with cognitive outcomes. The daytime sleepiness observation concerns a whole ketogenic versus low-fat dietary comparison in Parkinson disease. The studies do not isolate canola oil for sleepiness.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11276698/ | Copper overload and glial pathology discussion
assessment: Long–Evans cinnamon is the name of a rat model used in cited copper-homeostasis work. The review addresses Wilson disease and glial changes rather than exposure to ground cinnamon or Parkinson facial expressiveness.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4793296/ | Respiratory chain supercomplexes and part on fatty acid oxidation deficiencies
assessment: Potato mitochondria are cited in a respiratory-chain structural comparison. Dysphagia appears among symptoms of a mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation disorder. The Parkinson discussion concerns mitochondrial complex I.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9667037/ | Amino acid sources and microbiome mechanism discussion
assessment: Potato is cited as a food with a measured total free amino-acid content. The Parkinson review concerns microbiome-derived amino-acid pathways and models. The food composition entry supplies no exposure or clinical swallowing result.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11216301/ | Symptom terminology tables and discussion
assessment: Hot potato voice is a named symptom in head and neck cancer assessment, alongside dysphagia. The scoping review catalogs terminology, without a potato bolus or a Parkinson intervention.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11655668/ | Speech collection protocol and Table 3, ABLANDADA sentence
assessment: Participants repeat a Spanish sentence about a potato that is not properly softened as one phonetic test item. The Parkinson data are voice recordings from vowel, sentence, diadochokinetic and monologue tasks, without serving potato or assessing its swallowing effects.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11783828/ | Gut microbiome interventions and gastrointestinal symptom sections
assessment: Potato starch appears among isolated or blended prebiotic substrates discussed in the microbiome intervention section. The clinical focus includes bowel symptoms and the Lewy body disease gut literature. It does not test baked potato or quantify swallowing effects from the starch.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13197781/ | Neurologic gastrointestinal complications and Dickens epigraph
assessment: Swallowing difficulty is discussed as a complication of neurological and neuromuscular disorders. The underdone potato is in a quotation from Dickens, rather than a food bolus in a Parkinson swallowing study.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7614357/ | Household botany section, Margery's drawings and Henry's microscopy
assessment: Strawberries were the subjects of botanical drawings and seed microscopy in a historical household study. Writing and drawings are archival materials without a clinical handwriting outcome.

primary_locator: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10592043/ | Sister Study Methods and B-SIT analysis
assessment: The Sister Study compares polygenic Parkinson risk with a smell identification test in middle-aged and older women. It measures odor identification and genetic associations rather than strawberry ingestion or handwriting.
